submission.natural_language_explanation: This pole marks the beginning of a bounded span: it fires on the token that names the onset of a work, event, period or procedure (opens/begins/starts/began, kick off, launch, and the first/initial/introductory part of one) plus the following complement that introduces that span's first element ('with', 'by', 'at', 'in', 'on', 'the'), peaking on 'The video opens with…' (6.1), 'The film begins with a close-up' (5.1), 'The meeting began at noon' (3.3), 'His presidency began in 1933' (4.1), 'Let's begin the meeting' (4.5) and 'This is the first step of the process' (2.0). It stays at or near floor for the very same lemmas when they denote a physical opening ('He opens the jar/door', ≤1.4), a merely physical inception ('the ice began to melt' 0.6, 'the rock begins to crack' 0.8, 'the car began to roll' 0.6), an agent starting an unbounded action ('she began to cry' 0.1, 'he began to run' 0.6), an ordinal or rank ('he came first in the race' 0.1) or any ending ('ends/closes/concludes/finishes with', ≤0.6); its weaker negative pole fires on the mirror class of finality and later-part markers ('Finally', 'final', 'ending', 'summary', 'afterwards', 'Meanwhile').

It is a discourse/section-opening detector for written exposition, so it fires wherever a new section, topic or list is opened even without an onset word (for example 'The next section explains the method' or 'Part one covers the basics'), and its event and period examples are incidental.

It detects only the opening of a narrative or media work and its first parts ('the video/film/book opens with', 'the very first line'), so it predicts low on the start of a span that is not a work, such as a war, an office term or a meeting.

top_examples.text:
I’ve started playing with VoiceThread and love it! One class is investigating early animal domestication and are starting to comment on a thread called The Ancient 14.
Background the Students Had
14 large, herbivorous mammals were domesticated in ancient times. Of these 14, 12 are native to the areas in and around the Fertile Crescent. This amazing stroke of geographic luck meant that Neolithic man (and woman!) had a huge advantage in animal-powered farming. Only two, the llama and the reindeer, aren’t native to the Fertile Crescent and surrounding area.
I asked the students to choose one of the more obscure animals on the list then find two basic facts (when and where domesticated, for example) and one interesting fact (llamas don’t go into heat!).
Finally, the students either recorded their comment or typed a response. With just a 1/2 hour of student work I have a nice little slide show annotated with details.
We’ll add to the VoiceThread in the coming week to detail all the animals.
VoiceThreads, like YouTube videos, can be embedded in web pages.
Why not embed the VoiceThread in this blog? you might ask. WordPress.com, my blogging host, doesn’t allow much Flash embedding due to security concerns. If enough users request it and the WordPress.com gods deem it worthy, the feature may come along in the future. Until then, please follow the link to my class’ earliest VoiceThread attempts.

Free-access sow gestation stalls are designed to provide the protection of a standard stall and the behavioral freedom of a group pen. However, research is limited on actual implementation.
Research at the University of Alberta examined the effects of alley width on physiology, behavior and production of gestating sows in a free-access stall system.
After one month of gestation, seven sows were placed in pens with seven free-access stalls and a shared alley of 3-ft., 7-ft. or 10-ft. wide, where they remained until moving to the farrowing barn.
Health scores were recorded for backfat depth, body weight, body condition, lameness and lesions. Blood samples were collected monthly for cortisol concentrations and immune function. Farrowing production data was also collected.
The health and physiology measures showed very few differences between alley sizes.
Sows in pens with 3-ft. alleys used the space less, had fewer and smaller social interactions and were less active than sows with either 7 ft. or 10-ft. alleys. There were no differences in aggression between sows based on alley widths.
Neither sow productivity measures nor litter size differed between treatments. However, sows from pens with 3-ft.-wide alleys had heavier litters than sows with 10-ft. alleys.
Researchers concluded that alley width had little effect on sow health, physiology or production. But 3-ft.-wide alleys limited sow expression of normal behavior.
The research was supported by the National Pork Board.
Researcher: Ed Pajor, University of Alberta. For more information contact Pajor at firstname.lastname@example.org.
